content: Tuberculosis and malnutrition are intricately connected. Tuberculosis can lead to undernutrition due to increased metabolic demands and reduced food intake. Conversely, nutritional deficiencies can exacerbate the disease or delay recovery by impairing critical immune functions. Currently, there is no established evidence-based nutritional guidance for adults and children undergoing treatment for active tuberculosis. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of oral nutritional supplements in individuals receiving antituberculous drug therapy for active tuberculosis. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases and trial registries up to February 4, 2016, to identify relevant studies. They included randomized controlled trials that compared oral nutritional supplements administered for at least four weeks with no nutritional intervention, placebo, or dietary advice alone. The primary outcomes of interest were all-cause mortality and cure rates at six and 12 months. A total of 35 trials involving 8,283 participants met the inclusion criteria. The findings were as follows: Macronutrient Supplementation: 1. Six trials investigated the provision of free food or high-energy supplements. Only two trials measured total dietary intake, and both showed that the intervention increased calorie consumption compared to controls. 2. The trials were too small to definitively confirm or exclude significant effects on mortality (Risk Ratio [RR] 0.34, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 0.10 to 1.20; four trials, 567 participants; very low-quality evidence), cure rates (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.41; one trial, 102 participants; very low-quality evidence), or treatment completion (data not pooled; two trials, 365 participants; very low-quality evidence). 3. Macronutrient supplementation likely results in a modest increase in weight gain during tuberculosis treatment, although this effect was not consistently observed across all trials (data not pooled; five trials, 883 participants; moderate-quality evidence). 4. Two small studies suggested that quality of life might improve with supplementation, but the trials were too small to provide reliable conclusions (data not pooled; two trials, 134 participants; low-quality evidence). Micronutrient Supplementation: 1. Six trials assessed multi-micronutrient supplementation at doses up to 10 times the dietary reference intake, while 18 trials evaluated single or dual micronutrient supplementation. 2. Routine multi-micronutrient supplementation may have little to no effect on mortality in HIV-negative individuals with tuberculosis (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.60; four trials, 1,219 participants; low-quality evidence) or in HIV-positive individuals not receiving antiretroviral therapy (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.23; three trials, 1,429 participants; moderate-quality evidence). 3. There is insufficient evidence to determine whether supplementation improves cure rates (no trials), treatment completion (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.04; one trial, 302 participants; very low-quality evidence), or the proportion of individuals who remain sputum-positive during the first eight weeks of treatment (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.35; two trials, 1,020 participants; very low-quality evidence). 4. Micronutrient supplementation may have little to no effect on weight gain during treatment (data not pooled; five trials, 2,940 participants; low-quality evidence), and no studies have evaluated its impact on quality of life. 5. Plasma levels of vitamin A appear to increase after initiating tuberculosis treatment, regardless of supplementation. However, supplementation likely improves plasma levels of zinc, vitamin D, vitamin E, and selenium. Despite this, no clinically significant benefits have been demonstrated. 6. Notably, multiple studies on vitamin D supplementation at various doses have failed to show statistically significant benefits on sputum conversion. Authors' Conclusions: There is currently insufficient evidence to determine whether routinely providing free food or energy supplements improves tuberculosis treatment outcomes. However, such interventions likely improve weight gain in certain settings. Although individuals starting treatment for active tuberculosis may have low blood levels of certain vitamins, there is no reliable evidence to suggest that routine supplementation above recommended daily amounts provides clinical benefits.
